subject: system-design
question: An AP system accepts writes on both sides of a partition. What must it handle later?
options: Permanent loss of every write made during the partition
A mandatory two-phase commit after healing
Conflicting concurrent updates that need reconciliation when the partition heals
Permanent disabling of leader election
explanation: Accepting writes on both sides means the same data can diverge, so the system needs conflict detection and resolution.

subject: system-design
question: What problem does the transactional outbox pattern solve?
options: Atomically updating a database and publishing an event, so one cannot succeed while the other fails
Encrypting events at rest without a key service
Removing the need for consumers to be idempotent
Making reads faster by caching query results in a queue
explanation: The event is written to an outbox table in the same local transaction as the state change, then relayed to the broker.

subject: system-design
question: What is a sloppy quorum?
options: A write quorum that can accept writes on nodes outside the key's home replicas, weakening the overlap guarantee
A quorum that requires all N replicas to acknowledge every write
A quorum that ignores write timestamps entirely
A read-only quorum used only during backups
explanation: Dynamo-style systems use sloppy quorums with hinted handoff for availability, so R + W > N no longer guarantees seeing the latest write.

subject: system-design
question: What characterizes a metastable failure?
options: A failure caused only by disk corruption
A failure that resolves itself within one heartbeat interval
A failure confined to a single availability zone
The system stays degraded after the original trigger is gone, sustained by a feedback loop such as retries or cache refill storms
explanation: Metastable failures persist because the recovery mechanisms themselves keep demand above capacity.

subject: system-design
question: What does the CAP theorem say about a distributed data store during a network partition?
options: It must trade off between consistency and availability
It can guarantee both consistency and availability if replicas sit in one region
Partition tolerance is optional and can be dropped
It guarantees linearizable reads with no latency cost
explanation: Under a partition, a system must either reject or delay some requests to stay consistent, or serve possibly stale data to stay available.

subject: system-design
question: Why does requiring a strict majority of votes help prevent split brain?
options: A majority always holds the most recent clock reading
Two disjoint groups cannot both contain a majority of the same cluster, so at most one side can make progress
Majorities let every node read from disk instead of memory
Majority voting removes the need for replication
explanation: Any two majorities of the same membership intersect, so at most one partition side can win an election or commit.

subject: system-design
question: Why are compensating actions insufficient for some side effects, such as sending an email?
options: Email servers reject all compensating messages
Once delivered, the effect cannot be truly undone, so a compensation can only be a follow-up such as a correction message
Compensations must run inside the same database transaction
Compensations are only permitted for read operations
explanation: Some actions are irreversible in the outside world, so sagas must model them as forward-only steps with corrective follow-ups.

subject: system-design
question: In Raft, when is a log entry considered committed?
options: When the leader writes it to its own disk
When a client reads it back
When every follower acknowledges it
When the leader has replicated it to a majority of servers
explanation: Committing on majority replication means the entry survives any minority failure and will be seen by future leaders.

subject: system-design
question: What is the purpose of the term number in Raft?
options: It acts as a logical clock so stale leaders and messages can be detected and rejected
It sets the size of log segments on disk
It is the wall-clock time of the last heartbeat
It identifies the client that issued the request
explanation: Terms order leadership epochs, so a node that sees a higher term steps down and ignores lower-term messages.

subject: system-design
question: Why is using wall-clock timestamps for last-write-wins conflict resolution risky?
options: Wall clocks cannot be read by application code
Every CPU core must have an identical clock or the write fails
Timestamps overflow a 32-bit integer within a day
Clock skew between nodes can make a causally older write appear newer and win
explanation: Clocks on different machines are not perfectly synchronized, so the 'latest' timestamp may belong to the earlier event.
